def: Alcohols (R-OH on saturated carbon), phenols (OH directly on benzene ring) and ethers (R-O-R') are classified by position and number of the -OH or -O- group.
points: Alcohols are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary based on the carbon bearing the OH group.
Alcohols are also classified as mono-, di-, tri-hydric (one, two, three OH groups), e.g. glycerol is trihydric.
Phenols have OH directly attached to an aromatic ring carbon; cannot be primary/secondary/tertiary like alcohols.
IUPAC name of alcohol uses suffix '-ol' with locant, e.g. propan-1-ol.
Ethers are named as alkoxyalkanes in IUPAC, e.g. CH3-O-CH3 is methoxymethane.
Ethers can be symmetrical (same groups on both sides) or unsymmetrical (different groups).
formula: Alcohol: R-OH     Phenol: Ar-OH     Ether: R-O-R'

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["OH or O containing compounds"] --> B["Alcohol R-OH"]
  A --> C["Phenol Ar-OH"]
  A --> D["Ether R-O-R"]
  B --> E["Primary, secondary, tertiary"]

example: (CH3)3C-OH is 2-methylpropan-2-ol (IUPAC), a tertiary alcohol since OH is on a carbon joined to three other carbons.
tip: Clearly identify primary/secondary/tertiary before naming - this classification is often asked along with nomenclature.

def: Alcohols can be prepared from alkenes, aldehydes/ketones, or Grignard reagents, while phenols are mainly made industrially from cumene or from diazonium salts.
points: Alcohols from alkenes: acid-catalysed hydration (Markovnikov addition) of water across the double bond.
Alcohols from carbonyl compounds: reduction of aldehydes/ketones using NaBH4/LiAlH4 or H2/catalyst.
Alcohols from Grignard reagents: reaction with aldehydes, ketones or esters followed by hydrolysis.
Phenol industrially made by cumene process: cumene is oxidised by air to cumene hydroperoxide, then treated with dilute acid to give phenol and acetone.
Phenol from diazonium salt: aryl diazonium salt is hydrolysed with water to give phenol and nitrogen gas.
Phenol from haloarenes: chlorobenzene fused with NaOH at high temperature/pressure (Dow's process) gives phenol.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Cumene"] --> B["Air oxidation"]
  B --> C["Cumene hydroperoxide"]
  C --> D["Dilute acid treatment"]
  D --> E["Phenol + Acetone"]

example: Cumene process is the main industrial method: cumene gives cumene hydroperoxide on air oxidation, which on acid hydrolysis gives phenol plus acetone as by-product.
tip: The cumene process is the most important industrial method - write it with all 2 steps and name acetone as useful by-product.

def: Phenols are more acidic than alcohols because the phenoxide ion formed after losing H+ is stabilised by resonance with the benzene ring, while alkoxide ion from alcohol has no such stabilisation.
points: Both alcohols and phenols can lose H+ from the O-H bond, but phenol loses it more easily.
Phenoxide ion (C6H5-O-) has negative charge delocalised into the ring by resonance, spreading out and stabilising the charge.
Alkoxide ion (R-O-) has no resonance, negative charge stays only on oxygen, making it less stable, so less easily formed.
Electron-withdrawing groups (like -NO2) on the ring further increase acidity of phenol by stabilising phenoxide more.
Electron-donating groups (like -CH3, -OCH3) on the ring decrease acidity of phenol.
Order of acidity: phenol (pKa approx 10) is much more acidic than ethanol (pKa approx 16).
formula: Phenol pKa approx 10     Ethanol pKa approx 16 (lower pKa = more acidic)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Phenol loses H+"] --> B["Phenoxide ion"]
  B --> C["Negative charge delocalised by resonance into ring"]
  C --> D["More stable, phenol more acidic"]

example: p-nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol because -NO2 group withdraws electrons and stabilises the phenoxide ion further by resonance.
tip: Draw the resonance structures of phenoxide ion showing charge delocalisation into the ring - this diagram is key to a complete answer.

def: Williamson synthesis is the preparation of ethers by reacting an alkyl halide with a sodium alkoxide or sodium phenoxide, through an SN2 mechanism.
points: Sodium alkoxide (R-O-Na) is prepared by reacting an alcohol with sodium metal.
The alkoxide (nucleophile) then attacks the alkyl halide (R'-X) in an SN2 reaction.
Works best with primary alkyl halides since SN2 needs less steric hindrance; tertiary halides give elimination instead.
Can be used to make both symmetrical ethers (both groups same) and unsymmetrical ethers (different groups).
Phenols can also be used: sodium phenoxide + alkyl halide gives aryl alkyl ether.
This method is preferred over simple dehydration of alcohols because it gives unsymmetrical ethers cleanly.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Alcohol + Na"] --> B["Sodium alkoxide R-O-Na"]
  B --> C["+ Alkyl halide R-X, SN2"]
  C --> D["Ether R-O-R + NaX"]

example: CH3-O-Na + C2H5-Br -> CH3-O-C2H5 + NaBr (gives unsymmetrical ether methoxyethane).
tip: Always use a primary alkyl halide with the alkoxide in your example - mention this choice avoids the elimination side reaction.

def: Lucas test distinguishes primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols based on reaction speed with Lucas reagent, while the FeCl3 test identifies phenols by a colour change.
points: Lucas reagent = concentrated HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2; reacts with alcohol via SN1 to form alkyl chloride (turbidity/cloudiness).
Tertiary alcohol reacts immediately (turbidity appears at once) because it forms a stable carbocation fastest.
Secondary alcohol gives turbidity within about 5 minutes (needs slight warming sometimes).
Primary alcohol shows no turbidity at room temperature; needs heating to react.
FeCl3 test: phenols give a characteristic violet/purple/green colouration with neutral FeCl3 solution due to complex formation.
Alcohols do NOT give colour with FeCl3, so this test distinguishes phenols from alcohols.
formula: Lucas reagent: conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl2

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Add Lucas reagent to alcohol"] --> B["Turbidity at once - tertiary"]
  A --> C["Turbidity in 5 min - secondary"]
  A --> D["No turbidity at room temp - primary"]

example: Phenol + neutral FeCl3 solution gives a violet colouration, confirming presence of phenolic -OH group.
tip: Mention the exact timing differences for Lucas test (immediate/5 min/no reaction) - examiners check for this specific detail.

def: Alcohols undergo esterification with carboxylic acids to form esters, and dehydration with acid catalysts to form alkenes or ethers depending on temperature.
points: Esterification: alcohol + carboxylic acid, with conc. H2SO4 catalyst, gives ester plus water (Fischer esterification), reaction is reversible.
Dehydration of alcohol with conc. H2SO4 at high temperature (about 443 K / 170 C) gives alkene by removing water (follows Saytzeff's rule).
Dehydration at lower temperature (about 413 K / 140 C) with excess alcohol gives ether instead (intermolecular dehydration).
Order of dehydration reactivity: tertiary alcohol dehydrates fastest, then secondary, then primary.
Esterification needs excess acid/alcohol and removal of water to shift equilibrium towards ester (Le Chatelier's principle).
Esters formed have a pleasant, fruity smell and are used in perfumes and flavouring.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Alcohol"] --> B["+ H2SO4, 443 K"]
  B --> C["Alkene (intramolecular dehydration)"]
  A --> D["+ H2SO4, 413 K, excess alcohol"]
  D --> E["Ether (intermolecular dehydration)"]

example: Ethanol + acetic acid with conc. H2SO4 gives ethyl acetate (CH3COOC2H5) plus water, a classic Fischer esterification.
tip: Clearly state both temperature conditions for dehydration (alkene vs ether) - mixing these up is the most common mistake students make.
